steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction to a report on the security and privacy risks of client-side scanning. Place it in the history of the encryption debate, explain why it might look like a compromise, raise the key questions, and define the terms we use.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- History: governments trying to limit encryption
- Client-side scanning (CSS) as the new proposal
- Why CSS looks like a compromise (incl. Apple's proposal)
- Why the promise is illusory; open questions
- Our finding and prior work we build on
- Terminology and scope: content, targeted content, client vs server

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - PC -> encryption in software -> backdoor requirements for governmental decryption access

  - only policy stops expansion to other material; only lack of a software update stops expansion to voice, text, video

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Strong encryption became available to the public nearly half a century ago, and since then intelligence and law enforcement agencies around the world have tried to limit its use. At first they tried to restrict access to encryption devices. Then the PC was invented and encryption became widely available in software, so there were attempts to require backdoors that would give the government access to decryption. By the end of the twentieth century these proposals were effectively abandoned in most democratic countries. Since then several national intelligence and law enforcement agencies have instead tried to enlist vendors as surrogates to get access to encrypted traffic, either using technical vulnerabilities or covert court-ordered access.

Many current policy efforts do not try to provide decryption capabilities, but try to get around encryption entirely by scanning materials before they are encrypted or after they are decrypted. The leading proposal is client-side scanning (CSS). It is a phase change in the debate and it needs a different analysis from the earlier debates about government access to encrypted data.

At first glance CSS systems may look like an opportunity for a compromise approach to surveillance. Data can be encrypted end-to-end in transit and at rest (e.g., in encrypted backup systems), instead of being available in cleartext on services where governments can serve warrants. Because the user's device is involved in the CSS process there might be some sort of transparency, for example some cryptography could help verify properties of the scan before it runs, or limit the purpose or pervasiveness of the scanning. CSS may also give users some rudimentary control, since they may be able to decide what content can be scanned, or remove the scanning altogether. Apple's August 2021 proposal provides some of these properties. It was advertised as limited in scope, looking only for images of abuse certified as illegal under international treaty, as having elaborate cryptographic mechanisms to prevent leakage of non-targeted material, and as letting the user avoid scanning by stopping their Camera Roll being backed up to iCloud.

But when CSS systems, Apple's proposal included, are analyzed from a security perspective, it becomes clear that the promise of a technologically limited surveillance system is in many ways illusory. Communications can be encrypted, but users' data is still searched and scrutinized by law enforcement in ways that users cannot predict or audit. This raises some obvious questions. How is the list of targeted materials obtained? What stops other materials from being added to the list, like materials that are lawful but displease the government of the day? How is the discovery of targeted materials reported, and to whom? What safeguards protect user privacy and stop third parties from using these channels to exfiltrate data?

Existing device scanning products like antivirus software and ad blockers protect the user. CSS on the other hand acts against the user. Its surveillance capabilities are not limited to data in transit, because it scans stored data, and this takes surveillance to a new level. Only policy decisions stop the scanning from expanding from illegal abuse images to other material that governments are interested in, and only the lack of a software update stops it from expanding from static images to content stored in other formats, like voice, text, or video.

Besides the fundamental questions of whose interests are served and whether privacy and purpose limitation can be enforced, there are also technical questions about whether CSS can really be a safe and effective tool for detecting crime. Are the algorithms that detect targeted content robust against adversarial modifications? Can adversaries influence the algorithms to avoid detection? Can adversaries use the detection capabilities to their advantage (e.g., to target opponents)?

Finding
- no design space giving substantial law-enforcement benefit without unduly risking privacy and security of law-abiding citizens

Prior work
- US National Academies framework; 2019 Carnegie Endowment study; Paul Rosenzweig early CSS analysis
- after Apple's August 2021 announcement: Eric Rescorla (Mozilla), Kurt Opsahl (EFF), Steven Murdoch, Paul Rosenzweig, Daniel Kahn Gillmor (ACLU)
- our aim: more thorough technical analysis of CSS generally; Apple used top talent and still no secure, trustworthy, efficacious design

Terminology
- "content" and "targeted content"
- Five Eyes and Apple: CSAM images; EU adds terrorism and organized crime; text for solicitation and recruitment
- proposed UK laws: legal but upsetting speech
- capabilities get used: revenge porn, copyright

Client vs server
- own devices = clients; social media = servers; grey area: private vs public space
- home file server, E2E messenger = private; cloud backup/drives in the middle
- private space -> client; blog -> server even if personally hosted

steps.text:

Since then several national intelligence and law enforcement agencies have instead tried to enlist vendors as surrogates to get access to encrypted traffic, either using technical vulnerabilities or covert court-ordered access.

Many current policy efforts do not try to provide decryption capabilities, but try to get around encryption entirely by scanning materials before they are encrypted or after they are decrypted. The leading proposal is client-side scanning (CSS). It is a phase change in the debate and it needs a different analysis from the earlier debates about government access to encrypted data.

At first glance CSS systems may look like an opportunity for a compromise approach to surveillance. Data can be encrypted end-to-end in transit and at rest (e.g., in encrypted backup systems), instead of being available in cleartext on services where governments can serve warrants. Because the user's device is involved in the CSS process there might be some sort of transparency, for example some cryptography could help verify properties of the scan before it runs, or limit the purpose or pervasiveness of the scanning. CSS may also give users some rudimentary control, since they may be able to decide what content can be scanned, or remove the scanning altogether. Apple's August 2021 proposal provides some of these properties. It was advertised as limited in scope, looking only for images of abuse certified as illegal under international treaty, as having elaborate cryptographic mechanisms to prevent leakage of non-targeted material, and as letting the user avoid scanning by stopping their Camera Roll being backed up to iCloud.

But when CSS systems, Apple's proposal included, are analyzed from a security perspective, it becomes clear that the promise of a technologically limited surveillance system is in many ways illusory. Communications can be encrypted, but users' data is still searched and scrutinized by law enforcement in ways that users cannot predict or audit. This raises some obvious questions. How is the list of targeted materials obtained? What stops other materials from being added to the list, like materials that are lawful but displease the government of the day? How is the discovery of targeted materials reported, and to whom? What safeguards protect user privacy and stop third parties from using these channels to exfiltrate data?

Existing device scanning products like antivirus software and ad blockers protect the user. CSS on the other hand acts against the user. Its surveillance capabilities are not limited to data in transit, because it scans stored data, and this takes surveillance to a new level. Only policy decisions stop the scanning from expanding from illegal abuse images to other material that governments are interested in, and only the lack of a software update stops it from expanding from static images to content stored in other formats, like voice, text, or video.

Besides the fundamental questions of whose interests are served and whether privacy and purpose limitation can be enforced, there are also technical questions about whether CSS can really be a safe and effective tool for detecting crime. Are the algorithms that detect targeted content robust against adversarial modifications? Can adversaries influence the algorithms to avoid detection? Can adversaries use the detection capabilities to their advantage (e.g., to target opponents)?

In this report we explore possible answers to these questions. In the end we find that there is no design space for solutions that give substantial benefits to law enforcement without unduly risking the privacy and security of law-abiding citizens.

This report builds on the work of many others. We build on recent work by the US National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine, which gives a framework for evaluating policy or technical approaches for access to unencrypted content, and on the 2019 Carnegie Endowment for International Peace study on encryption policy, which gives a set of principles to guide solutions. We also build on Paul Rosenzweig's early analysis of the policy issues raised by CSS and some of the technical issues. Since Apple announced its scanning proposal in August 2021, several researchers and organizations have quickly analyzed it and the technology and policy issues it raises. In particular we acknowledge Eric Rescorla of Mozilla, Kurt Opsahl of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, Steven Murdoch, Paul Rosenzweig, and Daniel Kahn Gillmor of the ACLU. Our aim here is a more thorough technical analysis that covers CSS more generally. Our analysis also sheds some light on the design decisions Apple made. Apple did its best, with some of the top talent in security and cryptography, and still did not achieve a design for a secure, trustworthy, and efficacious system.

Terminology. In what follows we call text, audio, images, and videos "content," and we call content that a CSS system is supposed to block "targeted content." We need this generalization. The Five Eyes governments and Apple have talked about child sex-abuse material (CSAM), specifically images, when pushing for CSS, but the European Union has included terrorism and organized crime together with sex abuse. In the EU's view targeted content goes from still images through videos to text, since text can be used both for sexual solicitation and for terrorist recruitment. We also cannot just talk about "illegal" content, because proposed UK laws would require blocking online speech that is legal but that some actors find upsetting.

Once capabilities are built, reasons to use them will be found. Once there are mechanisms for on-device censorship at scale, court orders may require blocking nonconsensual intimate imagery, also known as revenge porn. Then copyright owners may sue to block allegedly infringing material. So we need to understand what is technologically possible with existing and likely near-future content-scanning technologies.

One issue of definition is what counts as a client and what counts as a server. Obviously your own devices, like desktop and laptop computers, smartphones, and tablets, are clients. Also obviously, social media and content-sharing websites are servers. Fully exploring the gray area in between is beyond the scope of this report. But a useful guideline for the grey area is a private space versus a public space. A personal file server in your own home, which is there to augment the user's private storage, is more like the internal storage of a laptop than like social media. An end-to-end encrypted messenger application is a private space too. But there are many systems in the middle: cloud backup, cloud drives, generic encrypted storage hosted in the cloud, and so on. Our analysis centers on whether the system is meant to be a private space, and if so we consider it a client no matter what the underlying technology is. On the other hand we would consider a blog a server, even if it is personally hosted, because it is generically available on the Internet.

Can adversaries use the detection capabilities to their advantage (e.g., to target opponents)?

In this report, we explore possible answers to these questions. In the end, we find no design space for solutions that provide substantial benefits to law enforcement without unduly risking the privacy and security of law-abiding citizens.

This report builds on the work of many others. We build on recent work by the US National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine, which provides a framework for evaluating policy or technical approaches for access to unencrypted content [3], and on the 2019 Carnegie Endowment for International Peace study on encryption policy, which presents a set of principles to guide solutions [4]. We also build on Paul Rosenzweig's early analysis of the policy issues raised by CSS, along with some of the technical issues [5]. Since Apple announced its scanning proposal in August 2021, several researchers and organizations have provided rapid analyses of the proposal and of the technology and policy issues it raises. In particular, we acknowledge Eric Rescorla of Mozilla [6], Kurt Opsahl of the Electronic Frontier Foundation [7], Steven Murdoch [8], Paul Rosenzweig [9], and Daniel Kahn Gillmor of the ACLU [10]. Our aim here is a more thorough technical analysis that covers CSS more generally. Our analysis also sheds some light on the design decisions that Apple took. Apple did its best, using some of the top talent in security and cryptography, and yet did not achieve a design for a secure, trustworthy, and efficacious system.

Terminology. In what follows, we refer to text, audio, images, and videos as "content," and to content that is to be blocked by a CSS system as "targeted content." This generalization is necessary. While the Five Eyes governments and Apple have been talking about child sex-abuse material (CSAM), specifically images, in their push for CSS [11], the European Union has included terrorism and organized crime along with sex abuse [12]. In the EU's view, targeted content extends from still images through videos to text, since text can be used for both sexual solicitation and terrorist recruitment. Nor can we talk merely of "illegal" content, because proposed UK laws would require the online blocking of speech that is legal but that some actors find upsetting [13].

Once capabilities are built, reasons will be found to use them. Once there are mechanisms to perform on-device censorship at scale, court orders may require the blocking of nonconsensual intimate imagery, also known as revenge porn. Copyright owners may then bring suit to block allegedly infringing material. We therefore need to understand the technological possibilities of existing and likely near-future content-scanning technologies.

One issue of definition is what counts as a client and what counts as a server. Obviously, one's own devices, such as desktop and laptop computers, smartphones, and tablets, are clients. Also obviously, social media and content-sharing websites are servers. Completely exploring the gray area in between is beyond the scope of this report. However, a useful guideline for the grey area is that of a private space as opposed to a public space. A personal file server in one's own home, which exists to augment a user's private storage, resembles the internal storage of a laptop more than social media. An end-to-end encrypted messenger application is also a private space. Yet many systems sit in the middle: cloud backup, cloud drives, generic encrypted storage hosted in the cloud, and so on. Our analysis centers on whether the system is intended to be a private space, in which case we consider it a client regardless of the underlying technology. On the other hand, we would consider a blog a server, even if it is personally hosted, since it is generically available on the Internet.
